title: Constitutional Semantic Engineering
description_html:
This paper introduces Constitutional Semantic Engineering (CSE), a software-engineering discipline for systems whose behavior must remain semantically admissible across execution, refactor, migration, automation, and governance. CSE begins from the observation that software can continue to run while its meaning decays: tests may pass while authority assumptions disappear, traces may accumulate without becoming admissible evidence, and documentation may imply standings that artifacts do not support.

CSE constitutionalizes existing practices such as Domain-Driven Design, hexagonal architecture, functional-core design, event sourcing, provenance, architecture decision records, and capability-based authority. It organizes software around explicit semantic locality, authority, evidence, refusal, standing, and non-claims. The paper provides a minimal formal model for governed transitions, receipt admissibility, standing transitions, and claim rules; defines canonical governance artifacts such as receipts, policies, standing records, claim ledgers, glossaries, and non-claim surfaces; and proposes machine-checkable invariants for effect separation, authority completeness, receipt binding, refusal totality, non-claim preservation, standing monotonicity, and replay determinism.

The result is a framework for building software that can be governed, audited, migrated, admitted, refused, and compared without semantic archaeology. CSE is especially relevant to agent-built systems, compiler/toolchain bootstrapping, governed AI systems, constitutional runtimes, and long-lived software expected to preserve meaning across substrate changes.
